title: How long can you leave a menstrual cup in? Up to 12 hours
description: How long can you leave a menstrual cup in? Up to 12 hours. Learn when to empty it, if you can sleep with it, how to tell it's full and how to clean it.
imageAlt: Mochi, a pink mascot, next to a menstrual cup and a small alarm clock
intro: You can leave a menstrual cup in for up to 12 hours, according to the FDA and Cleveland Clinic. Most people empty it every 8 to 12 hours, and sooner on heavy days. Twelve hours is a ceiling, not a target: the right timing depends on your flow, the size of your cup and the instructions that came with it.

how-long.title: How long can you leave a menstrual cup in?

paragraphs.first: A menstrual cup can stay in for up to 12 hours before you need to take it out, empty it and rinse it. The FDA says cups are typically emptied every 8 to 12 hours, and Cleveland Clinic gives the same 12-hour maximum. Some brands set a shorter limit, so the label on your own cup comes first.
paragraphs.second: Your flow decides how close to 12 hours you can get. On the first heavy days you might need to empty it every 4 to 6 hours to avoid an overflow. On lighter days, morning and evening may be enough. If you're new to cups, empty yours after 3 or 4 hours for the first day or two: you'll quickly see how much it collects and plan from there.
paragraphs.third: The 12-hour limit applies even when the cup isn't full. Blood that sits for too long starts to smell, and the cup should be rinsed regularly whatever the amount inside.

table.caption: When to empty a menstrual cup in different situations
rows: Check how much it collected to learn your flow.
Every 4 to 8 hours, or sooner if it leaks

Just before bed and as soon as you wake up
Keep the whole night under 12 hours.

how-long.note: If your cup's instructions give a shorter wear time than 12 hours, follow the label.

overnight.title: Can you sleep with a menstrual cup in?

paragraphs.first: Yes, you can sleep with a menstrual cup in, as long as it stays in for no more than 12 hours in total. Empty and rinse it just before bed, then empty it again as soon as you get up.
paragraphs.second: This is one of the main reasons people switch from tampons. The FDA advises against wearing a tampon for more than 8 hours, which makes a long night awkward. A cup gives you a few extra hours, so a normal night's sleep usually fits without setting an alarm.
paragraphs.third: If you sleep for longer than usual, or your flow is very heavy at night, a pad or period underwear as backup can save your sheets. Leaks at night usually mean the cup filled up or wasn't fully open, not that something is wrong.

is-it-full.title: How do you know when your menstrual cup is full?

paragraphs.first: The clearest sign that your cup is full is leaking. Cleveland Clinic notes that leaks usually mean the cup has been in too long and is full, or that it wasn't inserted correctly. Since you can't see inside while it's in, most people learn their timing over the first couple of periods.
paragraphs.second: Watch for these signs that it's time to empty it:

items.leaking: Blood on your underwear or liner, especially after a few hours of wear.
items.heaviness: A feeling of heaviness or that the cup has slipped lower than usual.
items.measure-lines: On the last change, blood reached the top measurement line or the air holes.
items.time: You're getting close to 12 hours since you last emptied it.

is-it-full.after: Many cups have measurement lines on the side, which turn each change into a quick check of your flow. The NHS suggests talking to a GP if you need to change your period product every 1 to 2 hours, which can be a sign of heavy periods.

left-in-too-long.title: What happens if you leave a menstrual cup in too long?

paragraphs.first: If you leave a menstrual cup in for longer than 12 hours, the most common results are leaks, a strong smell and irritation. Take it out as soon as you remember, empty it, wash it with water and a mild unscented soap, and put it back in or give yourself a break with a pad.
paragraphs.second: If you accidentally wore it for 24 hours, the advice is the same. Most of the time nothing more happens. Watch how you feel over the next few days, and see a doctor if you notice unusual discharge, a bad smell that doesn't go away, pain or itching.
paragraphs.third: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is much more often linked to tampons, but it has been reported with menstrual cups. A 2019 review of 43 studies in The Lancet Public Health found five reported cases after cup use. It's rare, and the risk can't be compared directly with tampons, but you should know the signs.
paragraphs.fourth: According to the NHS, symptoms of toxic shock syndrome include:

items.fever: A high temperature that comes on suddenly.
items.flu-like: Flu-like symptoms such as aching muscles, chills or a headache.
items.stomach: Feeling sick, being sick or diarrhea.
items.rash: A rash that looks like sunburn.

left-in-too-long.note: If you have a cup in and develop these symptoms, remove it and get urgent medical help. Tell the doctor you were using a menstrual cup.

cup-or-tampon.title: Why can you leave a cup in longer than a tampon?

first: A cup collects blood instead of absorbing it, which is the main reason it can stay in longer. Tampons soak up blood and the moisture around them, and the FDA limits tampon wear to 8 hours. See our guide on

first.label: how long you can leave a tampon in

paragraphs.second: In terms of protection, cups hold up well. The Lancet Public Health review found that leakage with a cup was similar to or lower than with pads and tampons, and in 13 studies about 73% of people wanted to keep using one after trying it.
paragraphs.third: The catch is the learning curve. The same review found that most people needed a few cycles to get comfortable with inserting and removing a cup. Cleveland Clinic reports that around 10% of new users notice leaks at first, which usually improves with practice or a different size.

items.wear-time: Up to 12 hours of wear instead of 8 for a tampon.
items.cost: Reusable for years, so cheaper over time.
items.waste: Much less waste than disposable products.
items.practice: Inserting and removing it takes practice.
items.cleaning: Emptying it in a public restroom is less convenient.

cleaning.title: How do you clean a menstrual cup?

paragraphs.first: Wash your hands, then rinse the cup and wash it with water and a mild, fragrance-free soap every time you empty it. Many brands suggest rinsing with cold water first, as hot water can make blood stain the silicone.
paragraphs.second: You don't have to boil your cup every time. The FDA says to sterilize it at the end of your period by washing it and placing it in boiling water, usually for 1 to 2 minutes. Cleveland Clinic recommends a few minutes in boiling water. Check your brand's instructions, let the cup dry fully and store it somewhere cool and dry, ideally in a breathable pouch rather than a sealed box.
paragraphs.third: When you're out and can't reach a sink, empty the cup in the toilet, wipe it with toilet paper or rinse it with a bottle of water, and wash it properly at the next opportunity. Some discoloration over time is normal. Replace the cup if it becomes sticky, cracked, torn or keeps a smell even after boiling.

who-should-check.title: Who should talk to a doctor before using a menstrual cup?

paragraphs.first: Menstrual cups suit most people who have periods, but some situations call for a quick conversation with a doctor first. The FDA and Cleveland Clinic list these:

items.iud: You have an IUD: a cup could interfere with its strings or position, so ask your gynecologist first.
items.after-birth: You recently gave birth or have a vaginal infection: cups are only meant for period blood.
items.latex: You're allergic to latex: choose a medical-grade silicone cup.
items.prolapse: You have a uterine prolapse: a cup may not sit in place properly.
items.pain: Inserting or wearing a cup is painful: stop and ask a healthcare professional.

who-should-check.note: Stop using your cup and see a doctor if you notice itching, a rash, pain or swelling.

change-reminder.title: How can you remember to empty your cup?

paragraphs.first: The easiest way is to note the time when you put your cup in and set a reminder for your next change, at 12 hours or earlier on heavy days. Cups are comfortable enough that forgetting one is common, especially on a busy day.
paragraphs.second: Mochi is a free, private period tracker for iPhone with a built-in change reminder. You start it when you insert your cup and it nudges you when it's time to empty it, with a discreet countdown. It works offline, needs no account and keeps your cycle data on your iPhone.
third: A reminder helps with routine, but never wait for it if you feel unwell. If you prefer pads on some days, our guide on

twenty-four-hours.question: Is it okay to leave a menstrual cup in for 24 hours?
twenty-four-hours.answer: No. Menstrual cups are meant to be emptied within 12 hours. If you've left one in for 24 hours, remove it, wash it and watch for unusual discharge, smell, pain or itching. Get urgent help if you develop a sudden fever, rash, vomiting or dizziness, as these can be signs of toxic shock syndrome.

twelve-hours.question: Can you leave a menstrual cup in for 12 hours?
twelve-hours.answer: Yes, 12 hours is the maximum that the FDA and Cleveland Clinic give for most cups. On heavy days you'll probably need to empty it sooner to avoid leaks. If your cup's label gives a shorter time, follow the label.

is-it-full.question: How do I tell if my menstrual cup is full?
is-it-full.answer: Leaking is the usual sign, along with a feeling of heaviness. Check how high the blood reached on the measurement lines each time you empty it. After a cycle or two you'll know roughly how many hours your cup lasts on each day of your period.

boil-every-time.question: Do I have to boil my menstrual cup every time?
boil-every-time.answer: No. During your period, wash it with water and a mild unscented soap each time you empty it. Boil it at the end of your period, usually for 1 to 2 minutes according to the FDA, or as your brand recommends.

gynecologists.question: What do gynecologists say about menstrual cups?
gynecologists.answer: Medical sources generally consider menstrual cups a safe option. A 2019 review of 43 studies in The Lancet Public Health found leakage similar to or lower than with pads and tampons and few safety problems. Doctors do advise caution if you have an IUD or a prolapse.

downsides.question: What are the downsides of using a menstrual cup?
downsides.answer: Finding the right size can take a few tries, inserting and removing it takes practice, and emptying it in a public restroom is less convenient. The FDA also notes that cups may interfere with an IUD.

pee.question: Can you pee with a menstrual cup in?
pee.answer: Yes. A cup sits in your vagina, and urine comes out of a separate opening, the urethra. You don't need to remove it to pee. If you find yourself pushing hard on the toilet, check afterwards that the cup is still in place.

menstrual-disc.question: How long can you wear a menstrual disc?
menstrual-disc.answer: Most menstrual discs also have a 12-hour limit, but the rules vary by brand, and some discs are single use. Check the instructions for your disc and empty it sooner on heavy days.
